title: Zuo's Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals
subtitle: The Great Righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals · The Rise and Fall of a Hundred States · Zuo's Spring and Autumn
description: "Zuo's Commentary" (Zuozhuan), also known as "Zuo's Spring and Autumn," is traditionally attributed to Zuo Qiuming, a historian of the State of Lu at the end of the Spring and Autumn period. With nearly 200,000 characters, it is the earliest extant chronological history, detailing the conflicts, wars, alliances, and figures of the various states over 255 years, from the first year of Duke Yin of Lu (722 BC) to the twenty-seventh year of Duke Ai of Lu (468 BC). Its exquisite narrative, vivid characters, and elegant rhetoric make it the pinnacle of pre-Qin prose.

route.title: Journey Through Zuo's Commentary: Feudal Lords Contend for Hegemony, Spring and Autumn Annals of Hegemonic Rule
route.intro:
The highest achievement is to establish virtue; the next is to establish merit; the next is to establish words.
Zuo Qiuming, a native of the State of Lu at the end of the Spring and Autumn period, was a contemporary of Confucius. In the "Analects," Confucius said: "Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of clever words, an ingratiating manner, and excessive respect; I too am ashamed of them." This shows their mutual understanding. "Zuo's Commentary" takes the twelve dukes of Lu as its chronological framework and records the political, military, and diplomatic affairs of the various states over 255 years. Unlike the subtle and terse language of the "Spring and Autumn Annals," Zuo's is known for its narrative power—it tells the gripping story of the mother, brother, and son behind the five words "Duke Zheng overcame Duan at Yan," and the strategy and magnanimity of Duke Wen of Jin's "retreating three she's" at the Battle of Chengpu. "The Spring and Autumn period had no just wars"—Mencius described the age this way. Yet precisely amid this endless cycle of campaigns and alliances, the basic framework of Chinese civilization was laid. Guan Zhong, Zichan, Yan Ying, Shu Xiang—these brilliant thinkers moved among the feudal lords, dancing on the edge of swords through rhetoric and wisdom. Let us enter the ruins of five Spring and Autumn period capital cities and experience that great age of contending schools of thought and clashing powers, twenty-six centuries ago.

stops.title: Stop One: The Ancient City of Lu in Qufu: The Rise and Fall of the Land of Rites and Music
stops.content: The State of Lu was the fief of the Duke of Zhou, Ji Dan, and the "host state" of "Zuo's Commentary"—Zuo Qiuming used the reigns of Lu's rulers for his chronology because he was himself a man of Lu. The Duke of Zhou established rites and created music, and Lu inherited this legacy, earning the name "Land of Rites and Music." "Zuo's Commentary" records much of Lu's diplomatic activities with other states and the gradual hollowing out of ducal power by the "Three Huan"—the Jisun, Mengsun, and Shusun families. The Ancient City of Lu in Qufu lies in Qufu, Shandong, with a city wall circumference of about 11.7 kilometers, making it a model of a Zhou-dynasty feudal capital. Its palace area, workshop area, and burial area are laid out in orderly fashion; the bronze ritual vessels unearthed bear clear inscriptions. The site systematically reveals the layout of a Zhou-era feudal capital, providing the most complete archaeological presentation of the principle recorded in "Zuo's Commentary": "The great affairs of the state lie in sacrifice and war." Lu was not the most powerful state in the Spring and Autumn period, but it was the highest in cultural standing. "All the Zhou rites are preserved in Lu"—so remarked Han Xuanzi upon viewing the books of Lu. Zuo Qiuming chronicled 255 years of the rise and fall of states using the reigns of Lu's rulers, and the stories of Lu in his work are especially moving—the sigh of "the meat-eaters are despicable" in the "Battle of Changshao," the warning of Confucius in "The Jisun clan is about to attack Zhuanyu," the dirge of collapsing rites when the "Three Huan" sidelined the ducal house. Confucius was born in Lu and in his later years compiled the Six Classics, setting eternal standards for all generations. Zuo Qiuming was also born in Lu, wielding his brush to record faithfully, transmitting the great righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals. This land nurtured the broadest and deepest humanistic tradition of Chinese civilization. Today, at the edge of the ancient city, the golden glazed tiles of the Qufu Confucius Temple gleam in the sunlight—the Land of Rites and Music, its torch inextinguishable.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Ancient City of Qi in Linzi: Capital of Hegemonic Power
stops.content: The State of Qi was the first hegemonic power of the Spring and Autumn period. In "Zuo's Commentary," the stories of Duke Huan of Qi and Guan Zhong occupy considerable space. Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan "to convene the feudal lords nine times and restore order to the realm." Confucius exclaimed: "But for Guan Zhong, we would likely be wearing our hair loose and folding our robes to the left, like the barbarians!" Guan Zhong's reforms covered politics, economy, and military affairs. The monopoly system on salt and iron he created—"official control of mountains and seas"—influenced China for two thousand years. The Ancient City of Qi in Linzi is located in Zibo, Shandong. The large and small cities cover over 15 square kilometers, making it the largest metropolis in the East at that time. The "Strategies of the Warring States" described Linzi as having "70,000 households... on the streets of Linzi, cart hubs strike each other, people's shoulders rub." The site preserves the remains of Duke Huan's Terrace, Yan Ying's Tomb, and other relics. It was here that Duke Huan convened the feudal lords in grand assembly to assist the Zhou house, and where Guan Zhong planned the great strategy of "honoring the king and driving back the barbarians." The famous passages about Qi in "Zuo's Commentary" are too numerous to count: "One drumming rouses the spirits; a second diminishes them; a third exhausts them" from the "Battle of Changshao"; Duke Qing of Qi's complacency leading to defeat in the "Battle of An between Qi and Jin"; the historian of Qi writing unflinchingly in succession—"The Grand Historian wrote: 'Cui Zhu murdered his lord.' Cui killed him. His younger brother continued writing, and two died. The younger brother again wrote, and Cui let him be." This spirit of protecting historical truth with one's very life is the most glorious page in "Zuo's Commentary."

stops.title: Stop Three: The Ancient City of Zheng and Han in Xinzheng: The Heart of the Central Plains
stops.content: The State of Zheng was one of the most active states in the early Spring and Autumn period. "Zuo's Commentary" opens with "Duke Zheng overcame Duan at Yan"—the gripping power struggle between Duke Zhuang of Zheng and his younger brother Gongshu Duan. Duke Zhuang's forbearance and scheming, Wu Jiang's favoritism and regret—Zuo Qiuming turned it all into the earliest brilliant narrative in Chinese literary history. Thereafter, Zheng navigated between the contending states of Jin and Chu. During Zichan's administration, he pushed through reforms and cast the penal code on a tripod, pioneering written law in China. Zichan did not tear down the village schools, keeping channels of public opinion open, enabling Zheng to survive and even thrive in the narrow space between the great powers of Jin and Chu. When Confucius heard of this, he praised: "People say Zichan was not benevolent—I do not believe it." The Ancient City of Zheng and Han (Including Han King Mausoleums) is located in Xinzheng, Henan. It served first as the capital of the State of Zheng (806–375 BC) and then of the State of Han (375–230 BC). The city site is an irregular rectangle with a wall circumference of about 19 kilometers, clearly divided into zones, including bronze-casting and iron-smelting workshop remains. The Han king mausoleum complex is vast, providing important material for studying Warring States burial practices. Zichan as portrayed in "Zuo's Commentary" is the most moving image of a statesman—he pushed reforms against the pressure of conservatives. On his deathbed, he told his successor Zitai Shu: "Only the virtuous can use leniency to subdue the people. The next best is severity. Fire is fierce, and people look on it with fear, so few die from it. Water is weak, and people play with it, so many die from it. Thus leniency is difficult." When Confucius heard of Zichan's death, he wept and said: "He was a legacy of love from antiquity." At the ruins of the ancient city of Xinzheng, you can still feel the warmth this wise man left behind. Zichan's vision went far beyond casting the penal code. He promoted people according to their abilities: Feng Jianzi could decide great matters, Zitai Shu was refined and cultured, Gongsun Hui understood the affairs of the four neighboring states—each was used to their fullest. Most admirable was his willingness to let the people discuss politics: the people of Zheng would gather at the village schools to debate the government. Someone advised him to destroy the schools, but Zichan replied: "When the people return from their work in the evening and gather there to discuss the merits and faults of the government, what they approve, I implement; what they dislike, I reform. They are my teachers. Why should I destroy them?" When Confucius heard of this, he praised: "From this I can see that when people say Zichan was not benevolent, I do not believe it."

stops.title: Stop Four: The Ancient City of Chu at Jinan in Jingzhou: The Glory of the Southern Hegemon
stops.content: The State of Chu was one of the Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period and the southern power to which "Zuo's Commentary" devotes the most ink. The story of King Zhuang of Chu—"three years without flying, but when he flies, he will soar to heaven; three years without calling, but when he calls, he will astound the world"—comes from Zuo's account. He inquired about the Zhou tripods: "The King of Chu attacked the Rong of Lu Hun, then proceeded to Luo, mustering his troops on the Zhou border. King Ding sent Wangsun Man to comfort the King of Chu, who asked about the size and weight of the nine tripods"—"inquiring about the tripods" became synonymous with coveting the throne. At the Battle of Bi, King Zhuang of Chu routed the Jin army, wiping out the shame of the Battle of Chengpu, and finally became a true hegemon. Shen Gong Wuchen opened relations between Wu and Jin, initiating the rise of the State of Wu—these brilliant chapters in "Zuo's Commentary" bring the hegemonic enterprise of Chu to vivid life. The Ancient City of Chu at Jinan is in Jingzhou, Hubei. From King Wen of Chu's move of the capital here until the Qin general Bai Qi captured Ying, it served as Chu's capital for four centuries. The city site is nearly square, with rammed-earth walls measuring about 15.5 kilometers in circumference and a moat outside the walls—it was the largest city in southern China at the time. The exquisite lacquerware, silk fabrics, and bronze vessels unearthed from the Yushan and Tianxingguan tomb complexes showcase the high material civilization of Chu. Without "Zuo's Commentary," our knowledge of Chu's early history would be a blank. Chu's official system—Lingyin, Sima, Mo'ao—Chu burial customs, King Zhuang's hegemonic enterprise, the ferocity of the Battle of Boju between Wu and Chu—all were transmitted through Zuo Qiuming's brush. Standing on the Jinan city site, the thousand-li waves of rice on the Jingjiang Plain rise and fall in the wind. The tenacity of the Chu people who "pioneered through brambles to open up the mountains and forests" 2,600 years ago seems to appear before your eyes. In his youth, King Zhuang of Chu seemed a dissolute ruler—"embracing a Zheng beauty in his left arm, a Yue beauty in his right, seated amid bells and drums." Wu Ju challenged him with a riddle: "There is a bird that has neither flown nor sung for three years. What bird is it?" King Zhuang replied: "If it has not flown for three years, when it flies, it will soar to heaven; if it has not sung for three years, when it sings, it will astound the world." Thereafter, King Zhuang astounded the world: he attacked the Rong of Lu Hun, inquired about the Zhou tripods in the Central Plains, defeated the Jin at Bi, and became a true hegemon. The figures of Chu in "Zuo's Commentary" are all vivid—Lingyin Sunshu Ao, incorruptible and self-disciplined; Shen Gong Wuchen, resourceful and strategic. The rise and fall of Chu is a grand epic of the collision and fusion of southern civilization with the civilization of the Central Plains.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Houma Jin State Ruins: The Last Testament of Hegemonic Power
stops.content: The State of Jin was one of the most powerful states in the Spring and Autumn period, and Duke Wen of Jin, Chong'er, was a legendary figure among the Five Hegemons. "Zuo's Commentary" records in detail Chong'er's nineteen years of exile through eight states—"When he passed through Wei, Duke Wen of Wei did not treat him with courtesy. He went out to Wulu and begged for food from a farmer, who gave him a clod of earth." Chong'er was furious and wanted to whip the farmer, but his attendant Zifan said: "It is Heaven's gift!"—Heaven was giving him territory! Chong'er then knelt, accepted the clod, and carried it in his carriage. Thereafter, the Battle of Chengpu routed the Chu army, and the Covenant of Jiantu established his hegemony. The Houma Jin State Ruins in Houma, Shanxi, are the site of Jin's final capital, Xintian. Duke Jing of Jin moved the capital here in 585 BC, and it served as capital for nearly two hundred years. Here were unearthed over 5,000 pieces of the "Houma Covenant Texts"—written in cinnabar on jade tablets, the earliest extant brush-written manuscripts in China—recording oaths among the Jin ministerial clans, including the Zhao family. These texts vividly recreate the political maneuvering on the eve of the "Partition of Jin by the Three Families" in the late Spring and Autumn period. "Zuo's Commentary" is extraordinarily rich in its accounts of Jin: Zhao Dun killing his lord, the Orphan of Zhao, the Battle of Bi between Jin and Chu, the Battle of An between Jin and Qi. Most astonishing is the scene from "Duke Ling of Jin did not follow the way of a ruler"—Chu Ni, sent to assassinate Zhao Dun, crept into Zhao's residence at dawn and saw him "dressed in his court robes, ready for the morning audience, but it was still early, so he sat and dozed." Chu Ni sighed: "He does not forget respectfulness—he is the steward of the people. To kill the steward of the people is disloyal; to abandon one's lord's command is untrustworthy." He then dashed his head against a locust tree and died. Zuo Qiuming's brush lets the human light of an assassin pierce through 2,600 years.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Qin Yongcheng Site in Fengxiang: The Beginning of Qin's Hegemony
stops.content: In "Zuo's Commentary," the State of Qin is a western power full of legend. The story of Duke Mu of Qin and Bai Li Xi is perhaps the most moving ruler-minister encounter of the Spring and Autumn period—Duke Mu exchanged five black sheepskins for Bai Li Xi, who had been reduced to slavery, and "entrusted him with the government of the state," thus beginning Qin's hegemonic rise. In 647 BC, when a famine struck the State of Jin, Duke Mu of Qin shipped grain eastward along the Wei River in a massive relief operation, known as the "Boat-Convoy Campaign"—boats set out from Yongcheng, sailed east along the Wei River, then north on the Yellow River and the Fen River, a spectacular sight. Yet Duke Hui of Jin proved ungrateful, and the two states eventually went to war. At the Battle of Hanyuan, Duke Mu of Qin captured Duke Hui of Jin, and Qin formally ascended to the stage of hegemonic power. In Zuo Qiuming's narrative, Duke Mu of Qin emerges as a ruler who could recognize his mistakes and act with leniency and benevolence—he ultimately did not execute Duke Hui but treated him with the courtesy due a feudal lord. The Qin Yongcheng Site in Fengxiang, Shaanxi, was Qin's capital for nearly three hundred years, from the first year of Duke De of Qin (677 BC) to the second year of Duke Xian of Qin (383 BC)—the longest of any Qin capital. The city site is roughly square, with rammed-earth walls approximately three kilometers from east to west and more than three kilometers from north to south, grand in scale. Within the site have been discovered ancestral temple foundations, a palace zone, and an ice cellar—this icehouse is the earliest cold-storage facility ever found in China, revealing the ingenuity and wisdom of the Qin people. To the south of the city site, in the Qin Duke cemetery, is the shocking Tomb No. 1 of the Qin Dukes—the largest pre-Qin tomb ever excavated, with a burial chamber covering over 5,000 square meters. Stone chimes unearthed from the tomb bear inscriptions recording the achievements of Duke Jing of Qin. The Stone Drums—China's earliest surviving stone-engraved text—were unearthed at Chencang near Yongcheng. These ten drum-shaped stones are inscribed with four-character poems in the Grand Seal script of the historian Zhou, recounting the splendor of a Qin king's hunt, with vigorous and ancient brushwork, hailed by Kang Youwei as "China's most ancient artifact." In "Zuo's Commentary," Qin is often dismissed by the Central Plains states as a "western barbarian"—yet the Yongcheng site tells us this was a state of high civilization and great power. From here, the Qin people expanded eastward step by step. A hundred years later, in the Xianyang era, they would unify the entire realm.
